title: Scene Builder
tagline: Get your first picture on the screen and learn how the computer finds any spot on it.
successMessage: You just built a whole scene out of nothing but numbers and emoji. Every game you'll ever make starts exactly here. 🎨

steps.title: Put something on the screen

seeIt.note: Right now your screen is empty. By the end of this step there's a cat on it.

getIt.title: How the computer finds a spot
beats: Every spot on the screen has two numbers: x (how far across) and y (how far down).
The corner at the very top-left is 0, 0.
Drag the cat around and watch the two numbers change.

explain.title: Every line, in plain English
explain.intro: Four lines, four completely different jobs. Once you know these, you can read the top of every game in this course.

lines.what: Fetches two tools — Game and Sprite — out of a library called stage.
lines.why: Python starts out knowing almost nothing about graphics. Anything beyond adding numbers and printing text has to be imported by name. stage is the little game library built for this course, and this line unpacks exactly the two tools you need from it. Ask for a tool you didn't import and Python replies NameError — it genuinely has never heard of it.

lines.what: Builds the stage: a screen 480 across, 360 down, painted midnight blue.
lines.why: The words inside the brackets (width=, height=, background=) are named arguments. Naming them means order doesn't matter and you can read the line back later without guessing what 480 was for. This line has to come first, because every sprite you make afterwards quietly attaches itself to the stage that already exists.

lines.what: Makes a cat 60 pixels tall, standing 240 across and 180 down.
lines.why: Notice what's missing: you never tell the cat to draw itself. Creating a Sprite adds it to the stage's list of things, and the stage repaints that whole list for you. This is the big idea behind almost every game engine — you describe what exists, the engine worries about pixels.

lines.what: Three ways of asking for the same cat. Use whichever you like.
lines.why: There is no key on a laptop that types an emoji, so every picture in the library also answers to a plain name you can type. "cat" is looked up the moment the sprite is built and swapped for the real picture. Anything the library does not recognise is handed straight back and drawn as-is, which is why Sprite("1UP") puts the letters 1UP on the stage — handy for scoreboards.

lines.what: Hands your finished scene over to the screen.
lines.why: Everything above only describes the game; nothing appears until this runs. It goes last, always — like pressing Send on a message you've finished writing.

steps.brief: Make a cat appear on the stage. A Sprite is any character drawn from a picture — you tell it which picture, where to stand, and how big to be. Your keyboard can't type an emoji, so every picture has a name you CAN type: "cat", "dog", "rocket". The full list is in "Pictures you can use" further down this page.
todo: Below the comment, make a Sprite using the picture name "cat".
Give it x=240 and y=180 so it lands in the middle, and size=60.
Press Play to see it, then press Check.
steps.starterCode:
from stage import Game, Sprite

# The stage: how big the screen is, and what colour the background is.
game = Game(width=480, height=360, background="#0B1020")

# TODO: put a cat on the stage.
#       A sprite looks like:  Sprite("name", x=..., y=..., size=...)


# Always the last line — it hands your game over to the screen.
game.start()
hints: A sprite is made like this, with the picture name in quotes first: Sprite("star", x=100, y=100, size=40)
Put your line AFTER the game = Game(...) line. The stage has to exist before anything can stand on it.
x=240 is halfway across a 480-wide stage, and y=180 is halfway down a 360-tall one. That's the middle.
steps.solution:
from stage import Game, Sprite

# The stage: how big the screen is, and what colour the background is.
game = Game(width=480, height=360, background="#0B1020")

# A cat, right in the middle of a 480 x 360 stage.
cat = Sprite("cat", x=240, y=180, size=60)

# Always the last line — it hands your game over to the screen.
game.start()

rules.label: There's a sprite on the stage

steps.successMessage: There it is! You just drew something on a screen with code.

steps.title: Put things exactly where you want

seeIt.note: One sprite is lonely. Time to build a night sky around it.

getIt.title: Small y is high up, big y is low down
beats: This trips up nearly everyone: y counts DOWNWARDS, not up.
y=0 is the very top of the screen. y=360 is the very bottom.
Drag the moon to the top-right corner and look at the numbers you get.

explain.title: Naming things, and why y is upside-down
explain.intro: Three new sprites, three new lines. The only genuinely new idea here is the label on the left of the = sign.

lines.what: Makes a moon AND gives it the name moon.
lines.why: The moon = part is a label you're sticking on the sprite so you can talk about it later — moon.x = 300 to slide it, moon.hide() to make it vanish. A sprite with no label still appears on screen perfectly well; you just have no way to ever change it again. Name the things you'll want to move; don't bother naming scenery.

lines.what: Big x is far across. Small y is near the TOP.
lines.why: Screen coordinates are inherited from how the very first computer displays painted: an electron beam swept left-to-right, then dropped down a line and swept again — so counting y downwards was simply counting how many lines had been drawn already. Fifty years later every screen on earth still numbers pixels that way. Maths class puts y going up; screens put y going down, and that mismatch trips up absolutely everyone once.

lines.what: Two stars means two separate lines and two separate names.
lines.why: Each Sprite(...) call builds one object. Reusing the same name twice would just relabel — the first star would still be on screen, but nameless and unreachable. In Module 4 you'll meet lists, which are how you handle fifty stars without writing fifty lines.

steps.brief: Add a moon high up in the top-right, and two stars somewhere in the top half of the sky. Remember: to put something high up, y needs to be SMALL.
todo: Add a moon sprite — Sprite("moon", ...) — in the top-right area, which means a big x and a small y.
Add two star sprites — Sprite("star", ...) — anywhere in the top half (y less than 180).
steps.starterCode:
from stage import Game, Sprite

game = Game(width=480, height=360, background="#0B1020")

# Our cat, already on the grass.
cat = Sprite("cat", x=240, y=220, size=60)

# TODO 1: a moon high up in the top-right (big x, small y)


# TODO 2: two stars in the top half of the sky (y smaller than 180)


game.start()
hints: Top-right means x is large (close to 480) and y is small (close to 0). Something like x=400, y=60.
Each sprite needs its own line. Three new sprites means three new lines.
Stars look better small — try size=20 or size=24 for those.
steps.solution:
from stage import Game, Sprite

game = Game(width=480, height=360, background="#0B1020")

# Our cat, already on the grass.
cat = Sprite("cat", x=240, y=220, size=60)

# A moon in the top-right: big x (far across), small y (near the top).
moon = Sprite("moon", x=400, y=60, size=44)

# Two stars in the top half — both with a y smaller than 180.
star1 = Sprite("star", x=120, y=90, size=20)
star2 = Sprite("star", x=240, y=50, size=20)

game.start()

rules.label: There are 4 sprites: the cat, a moon and two stars
Something is up in the top-right corner

steps.successMessage: A whole night sky, placed exactly where you wanted it.

steps.title: Draw shapes, not just emoji

seeIt.note: Your cat is floating in space. It needs ground to stand on — and ground is just a big rectangle.

getIt.title: A rectangle is measured from its top-left corner
beats: A Box needs four numbers: x and y for its top-left corner, then width and height.
Ground across the whole bottom = x=0, y=300, width=480, height=60.
Drag around and imagine where the corner of your ground should sit.

explain.title: Rectangles, corners, and what a colour code means
explain.intro: A Box is your ground, your walls and your platforms for the rest of the course. It's positioned differently from a Sprite, and that catches people out.

lines.code: from stage import Game, Sprite, Box
lines.what: The same import line as before, with one more name on the end.
lines.why: An import list is just that — a list, separated by commas. Adding Box costs nothing and doesn't slow anything down; you simply couldn't use a word you never asked for.

lines.code: ground = Box(x=0, y=300, width=480, height=60, color="#1F7A5C")
lines.what: A green rectangle whose TOP-LEFT corner sits at (0, 300), stretching 480 across and 60 down.
lines.why: Here's the trap: a Sprite is positioned by its middle, but a Box is positioned by its top-left corner. That's not the library being inconsistent — it's how graphics systems everywhere store a rectangle, as one corner plus a width and height, because that's the cheapest thing to draw and the cheapest thing to test for overlaps. So x=0, y=300, height=60 fills exactly the bottom strip of a 360-tall stage: 300 + 60 = 360.

lines.what: A colour written as three pairs of characters: red, green, blue.
lines.why: 1F red, 7A green, 5C blue. Each pair runs from 00 (none at all) to FF (as much as possible), so #FF0000 is pure red, #FFFFFF is white and #000000 is black. Every colour your screen can show is just a recipe mixing those three lights.

lines.what: A tree whose middle is at y=270, so its feet land near the top of the grass.
lines.why: Because a sprite is positioned by its middle, a 56-tall tree centred at 270 reaches down to about 298 — just touching ground that starts at 300. Half the size, added or subtracted, is the arithmetic you'll do constantly once things start colliding.

steps.brief: Add grassy ground along the bottom of your scene using a Box, then stand a tree on it. A Box is a plain coloured rectangle — perfect for ground, walls, and platforms.
todo: Import Box by adding it to the first line.
Add a Box for the ground: x=0, y=300, width=480, height=60, colour "#1F7A5C".
Add a tree sprite — Sprite("tree", ...) — standing on the grass.
steps.starterCode:
from stage import Game, Sprite

game = Game(width=480, height=360, background="#0B1020")

moon = Sprite("moon", x=400, y=60, size=44)
cat = Sprite("cat", x=240, y=270, size=60)

# TODO 1: add Box to the import line at the top

# TODO 2: grassy ground along the bottom
#         Box(x=..., y=..., width=..., height=..., color="#1F7A5C")


# TODO 3: a tree standing on the grass


game.start()
hints: The import line takes a list of names separated by commas: from stage import Game, Sprite, Box
A Box is positioned by its TOP-LEFT corner, not its middle. For ground at the bottom of a 360-tall stage, y=300 with height=60 fills the last 60 pixels.
To stand the tree ON the grass, its y should be a bit above 300 — try y=270.
steps.solution:
from stage import Game, Sprite, Box

game = Game(width=480, height=360, background="#0B1020")

moon = Sprite("moon", x=400, y=60, size=44)
cat = Sprite("cat", x=240, y=270, size=60)

# Grassy ground: starts at the top-left corner (0, 300) and fills
# the last 60 pixels of a 360-tall stage.
ground = Box(x=0, y=300, width=480, height=60, color="#1F7A5C")

# A tree standing ON the grass — its feet are just above y=300.
tree = Sprite("tree", x=90, y=270, size=56)

game.start()

The ground is down at the bottom
There are 3 sprites now, including a tree

steps.successMessage: Solid ground! Boxes will be your platforms and walls in every game from here.

steps.title: Sign your scene

seeIt.note: Real games put words on the screen — titles, scores, lives. Same tool for all of them.

getIt.title: Words are things too
beats: Text goes on the stage just like a sprite, with an x and a y.
Text is measured from its top-left corner, so x=16, y=16 tucks it neatly into the corner.
In Module 3 you'll use exactly this to show a live score.

explain.title: Words are things too
explain.intro: Titles, scores, lives, GAME OVER — every one of them is this single tool.

lines.code: title = Text("Cat Under The Moon", x=16, y=16, size=22, color="#FFFFFF")
lines.what: Puts words on the stage at 16 across, 16 down, in white, 22 pixels tall.
lines.why: The words come first, before any of the named arguments, because they're the one thing a Text can't do without. Like a Box, Text is measured from its top-left corner — which is why 16, 16 tucks it neatly into the corner instead of hanging half off the edge.

lines.what: Changes what a Text says, at any moment, even while the game is running.
lines.why: This is the whole secret of a live score. A Text isn't a picture that got painted once — it's an object sitting on the stage's list, and the stage re-reads its .words every single frame. Change the value, and the screen catches up 1/60th of a second later. You'll use exactly this in Catch the Fruit.

lines.what: White text on a near-black background.
lines.why: If your title never appears, colour is the first thing to check — white words on a white background are technically drawn and completely invisible. Designers call this contrast, and it's the difference between a readable game and an unplayable one.

steps.brief: Give your scene a title across the top. Text works like any other thing on the stage — it just happens to be made of words instead of pictures.
todo: Add Text to the import line.
Add a title near the top-left: Text("Cat Under The Moon", x=16, y=16, size=22, color="#FFFFFF").
Change the words to whatever you want to call your scene!
steps.starterCode:
from stage import Game, Sprite, Box

game = Game(width=480, height=360, background="#0B1020")

moon = Sprite("moon", x=400, y=60, size=44)
ground = Box(x=0, y=300, width=480, height=60, color="#1F7A5C")
cat = Sprite("cat", x=240, y=270, size=60)
tree = Sprite("tree", x=90, y=265, size=56)

# TODO 1: add Text to the import line at the top

# TODO 2: a title across the top of your scene


game.start()
hints: The import line becomes: from stage import Game, Sprite, Box, Text
Text takes the words first, in quotes: Text("My Scene", x=16, y=16, size=22, color="#FFFFFF")
If your words don't show up, check the colour — white text on a white background is invisible!
steps.solution:
from stage import Game, Sprite, Box, Text

game = Game(width=480, height=360, background="#0B1020")

moon = Sprite("moon", x=400, y=60, size=44)
ground = Box(x=0, y=300, width=480, height=60, color="#1F7A5C")
cat = Sprite("cat", x=240, y=270, size=60)
tree = Sprite("tree", x=90, y=265, size=56)

# Words on the stage, tucked into the top-left corner.
title = Text("Cat Under The Moon", x=16, y=16, size=22, color="#FFFFFF")

game.start()
